extracted.intended_audience: investigative journalists, IRE members, nominators and news organizations interested in entering or nominating for IRE awards
extracted.subtask_description: Landing page describing the Investigative Reporters and Editors (IRE) awards programs, what each award recognizes, eligibility/nomination information, and procedural notes (deadlines, placement of entries in the Resource Center). Useful for people entering contests or nominating honorees.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRE Awards — Recognizes best investigative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The IRE Awards is the annual contest of Investigative Reporters and Editors recognizing the best in investigative reporting by print, broadcast and online media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contest identifies top investigative work across print, broadcast and online media. Procedural note on page: 'The 2025 IRE Awards contest is closed. The deadline to enter was Wednesday, January 21, 2026.' After judging, all entries are placed in IRE’s Resource Center story library so that IRE members may learn from others’ triumphs and troubles. The contest helps identify techniques and resources used by the entrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philip Meyer Journalism Award — Best use of social research methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A contest that recognizes the best journalism done using social research methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint program of IRE and the Missouri School of Journalism (and partners). Three awards are given annually — a first, second and third place — to recognize the best work using techniques that are part of precision journalism, computer-assisted reporting and social science research. The contest helps identify the techniques and resources used to complete each story; entries are placed in the IRE Resource Center. Background/context about Philip Meyer and the emphasis on survey and social science methods is provided to clarify the award's focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Padlock Award — Most secretive publicly funded agency or person
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizes the most secretive publicly funded agency or person in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility: governments at all levels — from local to federal — are eligible. The award is handed out annually at IRE’s national conference. Nomination instructions: nominators will be asked to provide the name of the agency or individual along with reasons and/or media coverage detailing the intransigence. The page frames the award as calling out and bringing attention to governmental secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don Bolles Medal — Extraordinary courage in investigative journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizes investigative journalists who have exhibited extraordinary courage in standing up against intimidation or efforts to suppress the truth about matters of public importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established in 2017 in conjunction with the 40th anniversary of the Arizona Project, the medal honors journalists showing exceptional bravery. Nomination requirements: nominators will be asked to provide their name, affiliation and contact information, as well as details about the nominee — links to their work and a brief description of why this person merits the medal. Background on Don Bolles and the historical rationale for the award is provided to contextualize the criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRE Ring of Honor — Significant contribution to IRE and investigative journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrates members who have made a significant contribution to the organization and to investigative journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established in 2022. Nominations may be made in tribute to current or retired IRE members or in memoriam to deceased members. The program is positioned both as a way to thank contributors and as a fundraising mechanism to 'pay it forward' by raising money to help others. Procedural guidance on how to nominate and where to view honorees is provided on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of awards and prizes — cash prizes and dedication/FOI honors
rubrics_metrics.description: Every year IRE holds several different types of contests. Some have cash prizes while others honor dedication to (and against) freedom of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General note about award variety: some contests offer monetary prizes, others are symbolic or honor-based (e.g., for dedication to freedom of information or for highlighting secrecy). Contact information for questions is provided (awards@ire.org). The page also links to past winners and a winners' video to illustrate the kinds of work and honorees the awards recognize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination/application information requirements (award-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various awards require nominators/entrants to provide identifying information, supporting materials and explanations for why the nominee/entry merits the award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: Golden Padlock nominations require the name of the agency/individual and reasons and/or media coverage documenting intransigence; Don Bolles Medal nominations require nominator name, affiliation, contact info, links to the nominee's work and a brief description of why they merit the medal. For contest entries (e.g., IRE Awards, Philip Meyer Award) entries are submitted and, after judging, are placed in the Resource Center. The page implies that supporting materials and clear explanations of relevance/merit are expected.
